The topic of my talk is the role that environmental
sustainability can have as a strategy to build more
resilient data infrastructures in biodiversity science.
This talk emerges at the confluence of two sets
of consideration. The first set of consideration is
related to my current research, that is about sustainability in
research data management in biodiversity science.
I guess that many of you already heard about sustainability in this
context, but I think that in many cases,
you heard about it in relation to financial aspects.
In some cases, maybe also in relation to social aspects.
For instance, the
considerations about traditional knowledge and the role of data
that was part of one of the keynotes.
But I think that you-
Basically never heard it in relation to environmental aspects.
And yet, this is definitely something that should be
taken into account because research data management uses
IT infrastructures, and these IT infrastructures are
resource-intensive, and the environmental impact of these
infrastructures is also constantly increasing because we
have more and more data to manage, and also we are offering more and
more services to our users. And this means increased
electricity use and therefore increased greenhouse gas emissions.
Means also that we need more resources to produce hardware.
And in the end, this also means that we will have more e-waste
because we are now very bad at recycling electronic
equipment. The list could continue, but I think that this
gives an idea of why it is important to consider these
aspects. The second set of considerations
that are behind this talk are related to the fact that
we live in challenging times, and we cannot and should
not take for granted the unconditional availability of
key resources, energy, for instance, when we develop research
infrastructures. This is, of course, not my opinion.
It is what emerges from the reports of
policymakers. For instance, the most recent report of
the International Energy Agency, that is the organization that
survey worldwide the
energy situation. It is that there are three
critical aspects, at least three main critical aspects.
The first one is that energy demand is growing, but
the increasing geopolitical fragmentation and fragility makes
difficult to supply this energy that is required.
And
even if there were not this fragmentation, there
would still be problems because distribution
grids are not growing as fast as the requirements
that we have about energy. One key case, for instance, is
the sudden growth of the data center industry, driven by
the generative AI industry. And this is
definitely putting under pressure the electric grids
in many countries and not just in a few ones.
But this is just one of the weaknesses.
The other one important that is underlined and stressed
by the International Energy Agency is that
the supply chains of key materials are now under
pressures.
You may have heard that in 2025, China imposed an
export ban on rare earth elements, and these are key
in order to produce electronic equipment.
The European Union was not particularly pleased about it, and
I think that everyone has a sense of how much the prices
of electronic equipment have been rising in
recent times, and what this means practically when you need
this. But this is not the only problem.
There are also problem in provisioning, for instance, lithium for
producing batteries. So it is a whole lot of
things that comes together. And last but not least, the
International Energy Agency points out that
intervention to reduce global carbon emission and to
mitigate climate change and the risks that are
associated to climate change are not progressing
as much as expected. And this means in the end that we have
more risks to manage. And this is
why
resilience come into being. In my talk,
resilience in relation to research infrastructures
means the continued availability of the core services
in the face of political, legal, financial, and technological
changes. You may add more categories, but I think that these
four already make quite a good starting point.
And how do you build resilience? First of all, you need to decide
what are your core services, so what you want to protect.
Then you need to understand what are the risks
that
are a menace for your core services.
And then in the end, you need to have a risk management strategy.
And here comes the environmental considerations.
In 2023, the European Strategy Forum on Research
Infrastructures wrote a report on energy and
supply challenges of research infrastructures.
This report was written in the wake of the COVID pandemic
and of the Russian invasion of Ukraine that created so
much concern in Europe about the provisioning of gas in the
And the key recommendations that ESFRI
made for both national policymakers and research
infrastructures were to green operations, where greening operation doesn't
mean just consume less energy, but also think about
the materials that you need, especially the one that are rare and not
available on the market. Think about reusing and
recycling.
And the
reason for this is not because the
European Strategy Forum is staffed by convinced environmentalist, I
would say. The point is that they are policy advisors, and
as policy advisors, they see all the risks that are coming up,
and how thinking in terms of environmental sustainability
is simply a risk management strategy.
If you have a frugal infrastructure, this infrastructure is going to face
less risks when hardware is going to cost 10 times
more than it used to cost
a few years ago because
These are problems. The price of energy has also increased.
These are all aspects that should be taken into consideration.
And in the case of biodiversity data infrastructures, this point
should be very clear because biodiversity data are data especially
at risks. Because these are not just data for
scientists, they are data for policymakers.
In the European Union, where there is this concept of sustainable
financing, they are also important data for the financial
advisors. They are data with
a sort of political interest, as has been seen in
recent years, especially in relation to aspects like
environmental protection and climate.
So they are really data that can be contentious, and
these should be kept in mind. And of course, they also
face very material risks like energy prices
increasing,
unavailability of hardware or increasing costs for hardware.
But in the European Union, for instance, there are increasing environmental
regulations and there are also increasing reporting duties.
And this also puts further risks that are compliance and reporting
risks. And so this is when it comes into
being the value of environmental sustainability as a
risk management strategy. The recommendation that the
European Strategy Forum made in 2023 should be even
more heard by the managers of biodiversity data
infrastructures today in 2026, because it
is clear that the infrastructures that really keep
environmental sustainability in mind and so need less resources
are better placed to face the risks that are increasing.
And this is the reason why when I talk about these
aspects, people tell me, "Oh, environmental sustainability is a nice-to-have." No,
this is not the point. It's not a nice-to-have.
Even though you may not be particularly concerned personally
about this point, this is really a risk management strategy
because you need to keep these risks in mind,
and you need to have a strategy to face them.
And these risks are coming true. We see it every
day. So my take-home message is that you really need
to build the data infrastructure in biodiversity science with environmental
sustainability in mind if you want to make them more
resilient in the time of crisis that we are living in.
